Galvanized Pipe Replacement: When and How to Replace

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 5, 2026 · Updated November 6, 2026 · 5 min read

Short answer: Galvanized pipe replacement is usually a partial or whole house repipe with PEX or copper. Galvanized steel pipe rusts from the inside as its zinc coating wears away, which causes low pressure, rusty water and leaks. Angi puts a whole house repipe at about $1,500 to $15,000, typically near $7,500. A line that ever sat downstream of lead pipe is a federal replacement concern.

If your water runs brown when you first open a tap, or pressure has faded over the years, old galvanized pipe may be the reason. Galvanized pipe replacement solves both problems for good. SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local provider for repiping in Sarasota who can check your pipes and quote the job.

This guide covers how to spot galvanized pipe, why it fails and what replacing it looks like.

What is galvanized pipe?

Galvanized pipe is steel pipe coated in zinc. The zinc slows rust. It was common in homes built before copper and plastic took over. Over decades the coating wears thin. The steel then rusts from the inside, and scale builds up and narrows the pipe.

How to tell if you have galvanized pipe

  • Color. Dull gray or silver, unlike copper's orange-brown or plastic's white, blue or red.
  • Threads. Galvanized fittings screw together with threaded ends.
  • Magnet test. A magnet sticks to steel. It won't stick to copper or plastic.
  • Scratch test. Scratch with a key. Galvanized shows silver-gray. Lead is soft and shiny.
  • Where to look. Under sinks, at the water heater, at the main shut-off and in a crawl space or attic.

Signs your galvanized pipes need replacement

  • Brown water or rust flakes, mostly after the water sits
  • Low pressure in the whole house that got worse over time
  • Leaks at threaded joints
  • Rust spots or crust on the outside of the pipe
  • Uneven pressure, with some fixtures much weaker than others
  • Repeat repairs on the same lines

Why galvanized pipe raises lead concerns

Galvanized pipe can collect lead from lead pipe upstream. That's why federal rules single it out. Under 40 CFR § 141.84, water systems must keep a service line inventory. The rule names a category called galvanized requiring replacement. It covers galvanized lines that are, or ever were, downstream of a lead service line. If your utility contacts you about your line, this rule is the reason.

If you have galvanized pipe and aren't sure what lies upstream, ask your utility about your service line record. Ask your utility or the health department how to get your water tested for lead.

Galvanized pipe replacement options

OptionWhat it coversBest when
Spot replacementOne failing sectionOne leak, rest of the pipe still sound
Partial repipeOne area, such as a bathroom groupProblems in one zone
Whole house repipeAll supply linesRust, low pressure or leaks in many places
Service line replacementMeter to houseGalvanized line outside

Spot repairs on old galvanized pipe often buy only a short time. Connecting new copper directly to old steel can also speed corrosion. A dielectric union or another rated transition fitting keeps the two metals apart. Ask the provider how they'll join new pipe to old.

PEX vs. copper for galvanized replacement

PEX is a flexible plastic pipe. Wikipedia notes it's widely used for water supply lines and in repipes. It bends around corners, so it needs fewer fittings and fewer wall openings. Copper is rigid and long-lived, but it costs more and needs more joints. Both are common choices. Ask each bidder which they recommend and why.

How much does galvanized pipe replacement cost?

Angi's repipe guide, updated July 2026, puts a whole house repipe at about $1,500 to $15,000, with a typical job near $7,500. Partial jobs cost less. Home size, fixture count, pipe choice and wall repair all move the price. The repipe cost guide covers the line items to compare.

What happens during a galvanized repipe?

  1. Inspect and plan. The provider maps every line and fixture.
  2. Permit. Florida usually requires a permit for a repipe.
  3. Protect the home. Floors and furniture are covered.
  4. Open small access holes. In walls and ceilings where needed.
  5. Run new pipe. Usually through the attic in slab homes.
  6. Connect fixtures. New valves at sinks and toilets.
  7. Pressure test and inspect. The new system is tested and inspected.
  8. Patch. Holes are closed, often with paint as a separate line item.

Florida rules for replacing galvanized pipe

Florida places water supply work within a plumbing contractor's scope under § 489.105(3)(m). Use a licensed plumbing contractor and check the license on the DBPR site. While the system is open, ask the plumber to check pressure. The Building America Solution Center recommends keeping service pressure at or below 60 psi. A new pressure reducing valve may make sense if pressure runs high.

Galvanized pipe in Sarasota homes

Galvanized pipe shows up mostly in older Sarasota-area homes. In slab homes, the supply lines often run overhead, which makes an attic repipe practical. Older homes with a crawl space may be easier still. Coastal air can also rust exposed outdoor fittings faster. If you're buying an older home, ask the inspector to note the pipe material.

How to manage galvanized pipe until you replace it

  • Run cold water for a short while if it comes out brown after sitting.
  • Clean aerators often, since rust flakes clog them.
  • Watch for leaks at threaded joints.
  • Keep repair records for insurers and buyers.
  • Ask your utility about your service line record.

Local note: older neighborhoods in Bradenton and Venice are the most likely places to find galvanized supply lines. Older homes in Nokomis may have mixed pipe from past repairs.

Related reading: compare galvanized with polybutylene pipes in Florida and learn why your water pressure is low. Plastic supply pipe has its own issues, covered in CPVC pipe problems.

When should you call a repiping professional?

Call a pro when:

  • Your water runs brown or rusty
  • Pressure has faded across the whole house
  • You've had leaks at threaded joints
  • Your utility flags your line as galvanized requiring replacement

Frequently asked questions

How long do galvanized pipes last?

Life varies with water quality and pipe quality. Many galvanized systems in older homes have already reached the point of rust and low flow.

Is galvanized pipe safe to drink from?

It can collect lead if lead pipe sat upstream. Ask your utility about your service line and consider a lead test.

Can I replace galvanized pipe a little at a time?

Yes, with a partial repipe. Ask the provider how new pipe will join old steel to avoid faster corrosion.

Does homeowners insurance care about galvanized pipe?

Some insurers ask about pipe type and age. Policies vary, so ask your agent.
